content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
In the case of positive integers, we used a rectangular arrangement of objects to visually understand why the distributive property holds. We can use the same setup even in the case of integers by using green tokens for positive numbers and red tokens for negative numbers. For example, consider the following rectangular arrangement of tokens:
Figure: 4 rows, each of 2 green tokens and 3 red tokens, labelled 4 × 2, 4 × (−3) and 4 × (2 + (−3)).
We see that the overall arrangement represents 4 × (2 + (−3)), and it is clear that this also equals the sum of 4 × 2 and 4 × (−3).
Can you visually show the distributive property for an expression like −4 × (2 + (−3))? [Hint: Use the fact that multiplying a number by −4 is adding the inverse of the number 4 times.]
Thus, for any integers a, b, and c, we have a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c).

content.text:
Worked example: Read the rectangle for 4 × (2 + (−3)) two ways.
1. Row by row: each row is 2 + (−3) = −1.
2. 4 rows give 4 × (−1) = −4.
3. Block by block: 8 greens and 12 reds.
4. 4 × 2 + 4 × (−3) = 8 + (−12) = −4.
Answer: Both ways −4.

Block by block: 8 greens and 12 reds.

video_script.design: One idea: a negative number outside the bracket still spreads to each part, with signs. Assumes the sign rules and the distributive check with a positive number outside. Wrong idea: negative times negative written as negative. The anchor question stays all video; the first way and the second way stay from the ground part to the idea part; one clear, of the stage, before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip says negative two times negative three is negative six, because both are negative. The sign rule card, two negatives multiply to a positive, slides in and the negative six is struck.
maths_rules: First way, bracket first: 4 + (−3) = 1, then (−2) × 1 = −2
Second way, each part: (−2) × 4 = −8 and (−2) × (−3) = 6, then −8 + 6 = −2
sign rules used: negative × positive gives negative; negative × negative gives positive
The slip's slip: it writes (−2) × (−3) as −6, which would give −8 + (−6) = −14; the right value of (−2) × (−3) is 6
both sides are −2

concepts.concept_name: Distributive Property: (−2) × (4 + (−3))

content.text:
Worked example: Show −4 × (2 + (−3)) with tokens.
1. Multiplying by −4 means adding the inverse 4 times.
2. The inverse of 2 greens and 3 reds is 2 reds and 3 greens.
3. Four rows of 2 reds and 3 greens make 8 reds and 12 greens.
4. 8 zero pairs cancel; 4 greens are left.
5. Check: (−4) × 2 + (−4) × (−3) = −8 + 12 = 4.
Answer: −4 × (2 + (−3)) = 4
steps: Multiplying by −4 means adding the inverse 4 times.
The inverse of 2 greens and 3 reds is 2 reds and 3 greens.
Four rows of 2 reds and 3 greens make 8 reds and 12 greens.
8 zero pairs cancel; 4 greens are left.

content.publication_text:
Worked example: Show −4 × (2 + (−3)) with tokens.
1. Multiplying by −4 means adding the inverse 4 times.
2. The inverse of 2 greens and 3 reds is 2 reds and 3 greens.
3. Four rows of 2 reds and 3 greens make 8 reds and 12 greens.
4. 8 zero pairs cancel; 4 greens are left.
5. Check: (−4) × 2 + (−4) × (−3) = −8 + 12 = 4.
Answer: −4 × (2 + (−3)) = 4

End of chapter Figure it Out, Q14: Given that 207 × (−33 + 7) = −5382, write the value of −207 × (33 − 7) = ___.
1. 33 − 7 is the additive inverse of −33 + 7.
2. So −207 × (33 − 7) flips the sign of both factors of 207 × (−33 + 7).
3. Flipping both signs leaves the product unchanged.
4. So the value is −5382.
Answer: −5382

media.title: Pattern Machine
media.context: Class 7 'Operations with Integers', 2.2, Figure it Out (end of chapter). The one Doer tool of the topic 'Pick the Pattern: Rule Machines', placed on its last concept after the teaching, worked examples and videos. It applies the idea; it does not teach it for the first time. Interactive: the student predicts first, may make a move that does not work and sees its consequence. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description: Pattern Machine. One idea: A machine rule is an expression in a, b and c; a guess is kept only if it fits every row. Screen: A machine with three input slots and one output star, with the book's rows listed on the left; an expression builder with a, b, c, +, −, × and brackets; a Test button that runs the guess on every row and marks each fit; a Loop mode that feeds the output back in for the modified Collatz rule. What the student does: Guess a rule from one row and build it as an expression. Press Test to run it on every row. Change the rule until every row fits, then predict the missing output. In Loop mode, run the modified Collatz rule from a starting number and watch the path. Challenges: Machine 1: find a + b − c and the last output (−13). Machine 2: find −(a × b) − c and the last output (−111). The end-of-chapter machine: find a − b × c and the last output (−70). Loop mode: start at −7, −21 and −6; then start at 13 and see it return to 13. Build the largest and the smallest expressions from 3, −2, 5, −6 with +, −, × once each (60 and −60). Make your own machine and swap it with a partner. Feedback: A rule that fits some rows is kept on screen with the rows it misses marked, so the student can improve it. In Loop mode, a path that returns to an earlier number is drawn as a loop. The largest-value card keeps the best value found so far and lets the student keep trying. Done when: Three machines are solved, two Collatz starts are run including 13, and one machine has been made.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Pick the Pattern
Two pattern machines are given below. Each machine takes 3 numbers, does some operations and gives out the result.
Find the operations being done by Machine 1.
Machine 1: 5, 8, 3 gives 10; 10, 11, 12 gives 9; 5, 8, −3 gives 16; −3, 10, 2 gives 5; −4, −1, −6 gives 1; −10, −12, −9 gives ?
The operation done by Machine 1 is (first number) + (second number) − (third number).
Written as an expression, this will be a + b − c, where a is the first number, b is the second number, and c is the third number.
For example, 5 + 8 − 3 = 10, and (−4) + (−1) − (−6) = 1.
So, the result of the last group will be, (−10) + (−12) − (−9) = ___.

content.text:
Teaching plan:
1. Predict first: 5, 8 and 3 give 10. Which operations could do that?
2. Test a guessed rule on every row, not just one: a single row that does not fit rules the guess out.
3. Rows with negative inputs are the best tests, because they catch sign slips.

content.text:
Worked example: Test the rule a + b − c on Machine 1.
1. 5 + 8 − 3 = 10.
2. 10 + 11 − 12 = 9.
3. 5 + 8 − (−3) = 16.
4. (−3) + 10 − 2 = 5.
5. (−4) + (−1) − (−6) = 1.
Answer: Every row fits a + b − c: the outputs 10, 9, 16, 5 and 1 all come out.

• Brackets and the order of operations decide which expression gives the largest or the smallest value.

an odd negative number gives a positive result, because (negative) × (−3) is positive; an odd positive number gives a negative result, since 1 × (−3) + 1 = −2 and larger ones go further below

content.text:
End of chapter Figure it Out, Q5: Do you remember the Collatz Conjecture from last year? Try a modified version with integers. The rule is: start with any number; if the number is even, take half of it; if the number is odd, multiply it by −3 and add 1; repeat. An example sequence is shown below: −7, 22, 11, 32, −16, −8, −4, −2, −1, 4, 2, 1, and back to −2. Try this with different starting numbers: (−21), (−6), and so on. Describe the patterns you observe.
1. Check the example: −7 is odd, and (−7) × (−3) + 1 = 22.
2. 22 is even; half of it is 11.
3. 11 is odd: 11 × (−3) + 1 = −32. The book prints 32 here, but the rule gives −32.
4. Then halving gives −16, −8, −4, −2, −1.
5. −1 is odd: (−1) × (−3) + 1 = 4, then 2, then 1.
6. 1 is odd: 1 × (−3) + 1 = −2, so the loop 1, −2, −1, 4, 2, 1 repeats.
7. Start at −21: (−21) × (−3) + 1 = 64, then 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, and the loop.
8. Start at −6: −3, 10, 5, −14, −7, 22, 11, −32, −16, −8, −4, −2, −1, 4, 2, 1, and the loop.
9. Start at 13: 13, −38, −19, 58, 29, −86, −43, 130, 65, and so on; after 31 numbers it returns to 13, a second loop that never reaches 1.
Answer: Many starting numbers, such as −7, −21 and −6, end in the loop 1, −2, −1, 4, 2, 1, but not all: 13 starts a loop of its own, 31 numbers long.

End of chapter Figure it Out, Q15: Use the numbers 3, −2, 5, −6 exactly once and the operations '+', '−' and '×' exactly once and brackets as necessary to write an expression such that (a) the result is the maximum possible (b) the result is the minimum possible
1. For a large result, multiply −6, the number with the largest magnitude, by the most negative bracket of the other three.
2. (−2) − (5 + 3) = −10, and (−6) × (−10) = 60.
3. For a small result, make that bracket positive instead.
4. (3 + 5) − (−2) = 10, and 10 × (−6) = −60.
5. Trying every order and bracketing confirms that nothing goes beyond 60 or below −60.
Answer: (a) 60, from (−6) × ((−2) − (5 + 3)) (b) −60, from ((3 + 5) − (−2)) × (−6)

media.context: Class 7 'Operations with Integers', Figure it Out (end of chapter). The one Doer tool of the topic 'Pibs: Totals from Two Coins', placed on its last concept after the teaching, worked examples and videos. It applies the idea; it does not teach it for the first time. Interactive: the student predicts first, may make a move that does not work and sees its consequence. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description: Pibs Purse. One idea: A total is a signed combination of +13 and −9 coins; lists of multiples show which totals can be made, and making +1 makes every total possible. Screen: A purse of +13 and −9 coins that can be dragged onto a counter; a number line shows the running total; two ladders list the multiples of 13 and of 9 side by side. What the student does: Predict how many of each coin you will need. Drag coins onto the counter and watch the running total move on the number line. Use the ladders of multiples to plan a total before dragging. Write the total as a number sentence. Challenges: +85 (10 and 5). +20, +40 and +8. −50 and −2. +10 and +1. 1568 pibs: decide, and show one way. Make any price a partner names, starting from the +1 combination. Feedback: Every total is allowed; the number line shows how far it is from the target. Removing a coin is always allowed, so the student can undo and try again. Once +1 is made, the tool shows that repeating it reaches any price. Done when: All six cards are made, each written as a number sentence.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
An alien society uses a peculiar currency called 'pibs' with just two denominations of coins: a +13 pibs coin and a −9 pibs coin. You have several of these coins. Is it possible to purchase an item that costs +85 pibs?
Yes, we can use 10 coins of +13 pibs and 5 coins of −9 pibs to make a total of +85.
[Hint: Writing down a few multiples of 13 and 9 can help.]

content.text:
Teaching plan:
1. Predict first: a −9 coin takes value away. How could a purse with −9 coins help to pay +85?
2. Handing over a −9 coin is like receiving 9 pibs back as change, so a payment is (number of +13 coins) × 13 plus (number of −9 coins) × (−9).
3. List the multiples of 13 and of 9 and look for two that differ by the target.

one pair: 13 + (−9) = 4, so equal numbers of the two coins make only multiples of 4
break: 2 × 13 + 1 × (−9) = 26 + (−9) = 17, and 17 is not a multiple of 4

media.description: Terhüchü Match. One idea: Terhüchü, a capture game from Assam and Nagaland, played by two on one screen; a signed lead counter tracks who is ahead as coins captured minus coins lost. Screen: The Terhüchü board: a 4 by 4 square of 16 cells with its diagonals, a triangle at each corner and at the middle of each side, and two sets of 9 coins in the starting position; legal destinations light up when a coin is picked; each player's lead counter shows a signed number. content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Puzzle Time: Terhüchü
Terhüchü is a game played in Assam and Nagaland. The board has 16 squares and diagonals are marked as shown in the following figure. This is usually roughly scratched on a large piece of stone or just drawn on mud. There are 2 players, and each player has a set of 9 coins placed as shown. The coins in one set look different from those in the other set.
Objective: The goal is to capture all the opponent's coins. The first player to do so is the winner. A player may also win by blocking any legal move by their opponent. If a draw seems unavoidable, the player with more coins wins.
Gameplay: The starting position of the game is as shown above.
Players take turns. In each turn, they can move a single coin along a line, in any direction, to a neighbouring vacant intersection. Or, if an opponent's coin is at a neighbouring intersection, and there is a vacant intersection just beyond it, they can jump over the opponent's coin and land in the vacant intersection.
If a player jumps over an opponent's coin, it is considered captured and is removed from the board. Multiple captures in one move are allowed, and the direction can change after each jump.
Inside the triangular corners, which are outside the main square, a coin may skip an intersection and move straight to the next one. That is, it can jump over an empty intersection and go to the one beyond it.

1. The board: a square of 4 by 4, that is 16 small squares, so 5 lines each way and 25 points where lines cross. Diagonals join alternate points, and a triangle is attached at each of the 4 corners and at the middle of each of the 4 sides.

4. Keep score as a signed number: coins you have captured minus coins you have lost. +2 means you are 2 coins ahead; −1 means you are 1 behind.

- −9
- same signs: positive
- different signs: negative

Critical rejection conditions:
- a grid with other than 7 rows and 7 columns
- the lower middle column shown as 1, 2, 3 without minus signs
- any cell whose value is not the product of its two band values
- a quarter tinted with the other quarter's colour
- any count of tokens, cells, ticks, rows or coins that differs from the numbers stated above
- any token drawn without its plus or minus sign, or a plus and minus sign swapped
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame

Student takeaway: The sign of a product depends only on whether the signs of the two factors match; the sizes are the same in every quarter.

topics.summary: The sign rules for products and quotients, the three properties of integer multiplication, and the sign grid.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Summary
When two integers are multiplied, the product is positive when both the multiplier and multiplicand are positive, or when both are negative. The product is negative if one of them is positive and the other is negative.
When two integers are divided, the quotient is positive when both the dividend and divisor are positive, or both are negative. The quotient is negative when one of them is positive and the other is negative.
Integer multiplication is commutative, i.e., for any two integers a and b, a × b = b × a.
Integer multiplication is associative, i.e., for any three integers, a, b, and c, a × (b × c) = (a × b) × c.
Integer multiplication is distributive over addition, i.e., for any three integers, a, b, and c, a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c).
Figure: a multiplication grid with the row numbers −3, −2, −1, 1, 2, 3 across the middle and the column numbers 3, 2, 1 above and 1, 2, 3 below.

content.text:
Teaching plan:
1. The sign grid: across the middle are −3, −2, −1, 1, 2, 3; down the middle are 3, 2, 1 above and −1, −2, −3 below. The book prints the lower three as 1, 2, 3, but the products in those rows need the minus signs: the first entry of the row below the middle is 3, and (−1) × (−3) = 3.
2. Reading the grid: the top right and bottom left quarters are positive, the top left and bottom right quarters are negative, and every quarter has the same magnitudes.
3. Our opening prediction is settled: (−4) × (−2) = 8, shown by the token bag and by the patterns.
4. Still open for you: can you make a magic grid whose product is positive? Which starting numbers of the modified Collatz rule avoid the loop through 1?

objectives.objective_text: Students find two integers from their sum and difference by guess and check, record each trial in a table, and explain why swapping the pair turns a difference of 11 into −11.
Students find the pairs for all six given sums and differences, including negative ones, check each pair by adding and subtracting, and set a sum and difference puzzle for a partner.
Students trace two rightward strikes as jumps on a number line, find that strikes of 4 and 3 units end at 7, and write the final position as P = a + b.
Students write leftward strikes as negative movements, find final positions such as 5 + (−7) = −2 and the end of the movements 1, −2, 3 up to −10, and find a missing movement from the final position.
Students read three jump pictures to decide the direction of each movement and which magnitude is larger, and explain from the jumps why the coin ends left of 0, right of 0 or at 0.
Students subtract (+18) from (+7) with green and red tokens by adding 11 zero pairs before removing, and explain why adding zero pairs leaves the value unchanged.
Students argue with tokens that 7 − 18 = 7 + (−18) and 4 − (−12) = 4 + 12, and write additive inverses such as −(18) = −18 and −(−18) = 18.
Students subtract integers by adding zero pairs or the additive inverse, and use the fact that flipping every sign flips the total to find a long sum without adding it.
Students model 4 × 2 and 4 × (−2) by putting groups of tokens into an empty bag, name the multiplier, multiplicand and product, and find 4 × (−6) and 9 × (−7).
Students model (−4) × 2 and (−4) × (−2) by adding zero pairs and removing groups from an empty bag, explain why the removed tokens match the multiplicand, and test their opening prediction.
Students show that three different token sets for −2, each put in 4 times, all give −8, check 5 × 4 the same way, and find −4 × 2 by adding 2 reds 4 times.
Students find products such as (−5) × (−2) with the token bag, use 123 × 456 = 56088 to write signed products without calculating, and frame a sign rule for multiplying two integers.
Students describe how 4 × 3 down to 0 × 3 falls by 3 at each step, extend the pattern below zero to −3 × 3 = −9, and check that it agrees with the token bag.
Students extend the pattern 4 × (−3) down to (−3) × (−3) = 9, read the four times 3 tables, and state when a product of two integers is positive or negative.
Students show that 1 × a = a and −1 × a = −a, fill in swapped products such as −30 × 12, explain why multiplication is commutative, and match Brahmagupta's fortune and debt rules to the sign rules.
Students find products such as (−6) × (−3) and 10 × (−17) by the sign rules, find the integer whose product with −1 is given, and order six sums, differences and products of 348 and 1064.
Students write Mala's score as 30 × 5 + 20 × (−2), find 110 marks, and reason that the possible marks run from −100 to 250.
Students find the elevator's position after one hour as 0 − 180 and as 60 × (−3), and after 45 minutes from 15 m by both methods, reaching −180 and −120.
Students write signed expressions for a freezing room, cement profit and loss, and test scores, finding −18°C, a loss of ₹1000, 4000 bags, the numbers of answers, and the expression 8 + 4 × (−5).
Students play the grid by circling a number, striking out its row and column and repeating, then multiply the four circled integers, finding −30240 for the book's choice and for their own.
Students explain that each cell is a row number times a column number, so every choice multiplies the same eight factors and always gives −30240.
Students play the grid with their own choices, predict the product's sign by counting negative factors, and build a new magic grid from chosen row and column numbers.
Students reframe (−100) ÷ 25 as 25 × ? = −100, find the missing factor −4, and explain why the quotient's sign follows the multiplication sign rules.
Students find (−100) ÷ (−4) and 50 ÷ (−25) from matching products, and state the three sign rules for dividing integers with an example of each.
Students find signed products and quotients such as 36 ÷ (−18), fill in missing factors and dividends, and evaluate bracketed divisions, noticing when a quotient is not an integer.
Students evaluate 5 × −3 × 4 and 25 × −6 × 12 in several orders, find the same product each time, and state that integer multiplication is associative.
Students extend the series of products of −1, explain why each extra negative factor flips the sign, and state the even or odd rule for the sign of a product of many integers.
Students find long products such as (−2) × (−1) × (−5) × (−3) by counting negative factors, and find three consecutive integers whose product is −6 or 120.
Students work out 5 × (4 + (−2)) and (−2) × (4 + (−3)) both as a product of a sum and as a sum of products, and find the two ways agree.
Students read a token rectangle as both 4 × (2 + (−3)) and 4 × 2 + 4 × (−3), build the rectangle for −4 × (2 + (−3)) from inverse tokens, and state the distributive property for integers.
Students use the distributive property to find (−5) × (18 + (−3)), to get (−547) × 972 and its neighbours from (−548) × 972 = −532656, and to find −207 × (33 − 7) without multiplying.
Students test the rule a + b − c on every row of Machine 1, including rows with negative inputs, and find the missing output −13.
Students find Machine 2's rule −(a × b) − c by testing guesses on every row, fill in the missing output −111, and design a machine of their own for a partner.

Students find the machine rule a − b × c, follow the modified Collatz rule from several starting numbers and describe where it leads, and build expressions for the largest and smallest values and for given results.
Students check that ten +13 coins and five −9 coins make +85, write a total as a sum of signed multiples, and use lists of multiples of 13 and 9 to find a total.
Students make totals such as −50, +1 and 1568 pibs from +13 and −9 coins, check each with signed multiplication, and explain why making +1 means any price can be paid.

Students restate the sign rules for products and quotients and the commutative, associative and distributive properties, read the multiplication sign grid, and check their opening prediction for (−4) × (−2).

tool_pibs_purse.idea: A total is a signed combination of +13 and −9 coins; lists of multiples show which totals can be made, and making +1 makes every total possible.
tool_pibs_purse.title: Pibs Purse

tool_terhuchu_match.idea: Terhüchü, a capture game from Assam and Nagaland, played by two on one screen; a signed lead counter tracks who is ahead as coins captured minus coins lost.
tool_terhuchu_match.title: Terhüchü Match

tool_zero_pair_tray.idea: A zero pair is worth nothing, so putting in zero pairs lets you remove tokens that are not there; subtracting an integer gives the same result as adding its additive inverse.
tool_zero_pair_tray.title: Zero Pair Tray

tool_pattern_machine.idea: A machine rule is an expression in a, b and c; a guess is kept only if it fits every row.
tool_pattern_machine.title: Pattern Machine

tool_carrom_strike_line.idea: A strike is a signed movement: its magnitude is the distance and its sign the direction; two strikes end at P = a + b, and comparing jump lengths tells which side of 0 the coin stops on.
tool_carrom_strike_line.title: Carrom Strike Line

tool_sign_counter_chain.idea: Factors can be grouped and ordered freely; an even count of negative factors gives a positive product and an odd count a negative one.
tool_sign_counter_chain.title: Sign Counter Chain

tool_mine_shaft_elevator.idea: A signed rate times a count gives a signed change; adding the change to the start gives the end.
tool_mine_shaft_elevator.title: Mine Shaft Elevator

tool_sign_pattern_ladder.idea: Going down a multiplication ladder one step changes the product by the multiplicand, and the pattern continues past zero, which fixes the sign rules.
tool_sign_pattern_ladder.title: Sign Pattern Ladder

tool_token_bag_multiplier.idea: The multiplier's sign says put in or take out, the multiplicand says which group, and what is left in the bag after zero pairs cancel is the product.
tool_token_bag_multiplier.title: Token Bag Multiplier

tool_missing_factor_finder.idea: a ÷ b is the missing factor in b × ? = a, so the multiplication sign rules decide every quotient.
tool_missing_factor_finder.title: Missing Factor Finder

tool_sum_difference_finder.idea: Two integers are fixed by their sum and their difference; moving 1 from the second number to the first keeps the sum and raises the difference by 2, and swapping the pair flips the sign of the difference.
tool_sum_difference_finder.title: Sum and Difference Finder

tool_circle_and_strike_grid.idea: Each cell is a row number times a column number, so every legal choice multiplies the same eight factors.
tool_circle_and_strike_grid.title: Circle and Strike Grid

tool_token_rectangle_splitter.idea: A token rectangle of a rows and (b + c) columns equals the sum of its two blocks, so a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c for all integers.
tool_token_rectangle_splitter.title: Token Rectangle Splitter

misconceptions.text: The difference is always the bigger number minus the smaller one, so it can never be negative.
Ignoring the sign: reading −4 as 4 units to the right, or thinking −5 is bigger than −2.
Thinking that putting in zero pairs changes the value of the tokens.
Treating subtracting a negative as subtracting: 3 − (−4) taken as −1 instead of 7.
Two negatives make a negative: (−4) × (−2) taken as −8.
A negative multiplier has no meaning, or the wrong colour of token is taken out.
Dropping the sign of a rate, so a descent or a loss is added as a gain.
Believing division has different sign rules: (−100) ÷ (−4) taken as −25.
Deciding the sign of a long product from its last factor, or from any single negative factor.
Multiplying only the first part of a sum: a × (b + c) taken as a × b + c.
Accepting a machine rule as soon as one row fits.
Believing a negative coin can never help to pay a positive price.

chapter_approach.intro: Integers were added and subtracted in Grade 6. This chapter gives meaning to multiplying and dividing them. Every topic runs the same arc: play first, notice, name, reason, apply. The student always commits to a prediction before the answer is shown, because a sign guessed and then tested is remembered; a sign told is forgotten.

points.text: Products with negative numbers are built with a token bag and confirmed by patterns before any sign rule is stated. The rule is the summary of what the student has already seen.
points.title: Model before rule

points.text: Every product and quotient is found in two parts: multiply or divide the magnitudes, then decide the sign by whether the signs agree. Long products count their negative factors.
points.title: Sign and magnitude, separately

points.text: Subtraction and negative multipliers both work by first putting zero pairs into the tray or bag. The zero pair is highlighted every time it is used.
points.title: Zero pairs are the key move

points.text: Each concept opens with a prediction; every walkthrough video pauses before each reveal; every tool asks for a guess before the student manipulates.
points.title: Predict, then reveal

points.text: Each topic closes with Pull it together and do it: the recap, the chapter's exercises for that idea, and ONE interactive tool in which the student applies it. The tool never replaces the teaching.
points.title: One tool, at the end of each idea

points.text: No video or image from earlier plans is reused. Every video and image here is a new specification written for this plan and waiting to be produced.
points.title: All media are new
